item.title: States, voting rights groups renew challenges to Trump plans to restrict mail-in voting
item.description:
Democratic-led states and voting rights groups on Wednesday renewed their efforts to block the U.S. Postal Service from imposing new requirements for mail-in voting before ballots go out for the November congressional elections, as ordered by President Donald Trump. Democratic attorneys general from 23 states and the District of Columbia, along with Pennsylvania’s governor, filed a newlawsuit in Boston federal court two days after the U.S. Supreme Court lifted an earlier injunction they had won blocking Trump’s order on the grounds that they sued too soon.

item.description:

item.title: American Samoa’s Latter-day Saints temple dedication, open house dates planned
item.description:
By 
Joel Randall, Church News reporter
Source: Deseret Church News

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The Pago Pago American Samoa Temple was first announced in 1977. Now half a century later, it’s nearly complete.

Elder Quentin L. Cook of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles will dedicate the Pago Pago American Samoa Temple  on Sunday, Dec. 13.

The dedication — broadcast to all congregations in the temple district — will follow a public open house from Wednesday, Nov. 4, to Saturday, Nov. 21, excluding Sundays.

A media day will be held Nov. 2, and invited guests will tour the temple Nov. 3.

These dates were published Monday, Aug. 24, on ChurchofJesusChrist.org.

It’ll be the first temple dedicated in the United States territory of American Samoa. With dedication dates as currently announced by the Church, this would be the final temple dedicated in 2026.

ABOUT THE PAGO PAGO TEMPLE

Ground was broken for the Pago Pago temple on Oct. 30, 2021. Elder K. Brett Nattress, a General Authority Seventy and then first counselor in the Church’s Pacific Area presidency, presided over the ceremony.

“As we symbolically turn the soil,” he said, “let us turn our hearts to our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ. Let us establish a firm foundation in our Savior.”

The Pago Pago temple plans call for a single-story, 17,000-square-foot building, located in Tafuna, American Samoa, along with housing for the temple president and missionaries and a distribution center.

THE CHURCH IN AMERICAN SAMOA

Missionary work began in present-day American Samoa in June 1888, with the opening of the Samoan Mission. Before American Samoa became a U.S. territory in 1900, the first meetinghouse constructed in Samoa was dedicated Oct. 28, 1888, in Aunu‘u. A branch was organized the same day.

On June 15, 1969, the Pago Pago Stake — the first in American Samoa — was created. From 1985 to 1991, Church membership doubled from about 5,500 members to around 11,000.

Today, American Samoa is home to more than 17,600 Latter-day Saints, meeting across 44 wards and branches.

item.title: NOAA Ocean Exploration: Where We’ve Been, Where We’re Going
item.description:
Source: NOAA Ocean Exploration

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — On Thursday, August 20, NOAA Ship Okeanos Explorer left Rarotonga in the Cook Islands to begin a 29-day expedition to map and explore deep waters in and around American Samoa. During the expedition, the mission team will conduct remotely operated vehicle, or ROV, dives to explore the seafloor and water column and overnight mapping operations, and continuous shore-side participation via telepresence technology.

We expect to explore abyssal plain environments, with a focus on developing a baseline assessment of marine critical minerals, specifically polymetallic nodules, as well as seamount habitats, deep-sea coral and sponge communities, fish habitats, and the water column.Thanks to telepresence technology, NOAA Ocean Exploration invites anyone with an internet connection to watch and listen as members of the science community actively engage and guide each dive.

Today, August 24, the team will conduct the first dive of the expedition on a seamount near the boundary between American Samoa and the Cook Islands. They expect to launch the ROV at approximately 8:30 a.m. SST (3:30 p.m. EDT) and descend nearly 2,400 meters (1.5 miles) below the surface, to reveal the geology and marine life of this underwater mountain.

Barring any weather or technical issues, dives will be conducted daily August 24-September 1 and September 2-September 12. Most days, we expect to deploy the ROV at approximately 8 a.m. SST (3 p.m. EDT), but we’ll share updates if things change.

Join us live at oceanexplorer.noaa.gov!

This week’s tentative 2026 American Samoa ROV + Mapping expedition schedule
NOTE: All dates, times, and locations are subject to change

August 24: Dive 01 (8:30 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. SST): Seamount Dive
August 25: Dive 02 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive
August 26: Dive 03 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive
August 27: Dive 04 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive
August 28: Dive 05 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive
August 29: Dive 06 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive
August 30: Dive 07 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m. SST): Abyssal Plain Dive

 

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
NOAA Ocean Exploration

item.title: Obituaries for August 25
item.description:
Filomena Longboy Badua, 82, of Kapaau died Aug. 3 at home. Born in San Nicolas, Ilocos Norte, Philippines, she was retired from Mauna Kea Beach Hotel and a member of St. Augustine’s Episcopal Church and Kohala Filipino Community Club. Visitation with all-night vigil 6 p.m. Friday, Sep. 18 at the family home on Maulili Road. Visitation again 9-10 a.m. Saturday, Sep. 19 at St. Augustine’s Episcopal Church. Funeral Mass at 10 a.m. Burial at Hawi County Cemetery. Lunch to follow. Casual attire. Survived by sons, Bernie Badua, Edison (Sunshine) Badua of Kauai and Dennis (Florence) Pascua; daughters, Evelyn (Melvyn Ventura) Macalma and Mary Jane (Wilfred Jr.) Sulliban; brother Agustin Longboy; 14 grandchildren; and 13 great-grandchildren. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for August 25 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: ASCC expresses condolences at the passing of Cherylmoanamarie Ripley
item.description:
By 
ASCC Staff

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA —  The American Samoa Community College has joined the family and friends of Ms. Cherylmoanamarie “Cherie” Ripley in mourning her passing earlier this month. Until her retirement in 2024, Ms. Ripley contributed decades of service to the College, and was recognized by many as one of the pillars of its day-to-day operations. She was by far the most experienced of the College’s administrative staff, and is remembered for her in-depth knowledge and congenial personality.

Ms. Ripley’s tenure with ASCC dates all the way back to 1977, when she took the position of Secretary to the President. After three years with the Office of the President, Ms. Ripley transitioned to another secretarial role with the Instructional Support Division, under which she also served as an Administrative Assistant and Computer Lab monitor. In 1985 she joined the College’s Adult Education Department, once again as an Administrative Assistant, a title she took with her in her next transition to the Office of the Dean of Instruction in 1997. In 2003, Ms. Ripley joined the Institutional Affairs Division as its Website Administrator, serving until she became Special Assistant to the Dean of Academic Affairs four years later. Ms. Ripley remained with the Division of Academic Affairs until her retirement in 2024.

ASCC Dean of Academic Affairs Dr. Siamaua Ropeti, with whom Ms. Ripley spent her final years at the College, still expresses appreciation for her expertise. “As my special assistant”, recalled Dean Ropeti, “Cherie faithfully executed her role in all capacities, encompassing responsibilities such as initiating contracts, submitting time sheets and memos on behalf of the Division, doing waivers, assisting with graduation, preparation for Orientation and so much more.  

“Even after she retired, she continued to visit ASCC and mingle with her friends and colleagues until she was no longer able to do so. We still feel her presence, and take inspiration from her selfless dedication, her tautua to any fa'alavelave involving ASCC employees, and her commitment to order, instruction and quality service.

“To people who knew her, she was the epitome of professionalism. Our office considered her the elder sister, the advisor, and the glue that held the Division of Academic Affairs Office together. She will never be forgotten.”

Looking back on her decades with ASCC, as she prepared to retire, Ms. Ripley wrote in a 2024 letter to then-President Dr. Rosevonne Makaiwi-Pato, “I will be tossing in the towel from my post as ASCC Special Administrative Assistant to the Dean of Academic Affairs.  I will be leaving the Halls of Ivy of the American Samoa Community College after almost 50 years of dedication and returning to Sogi, Leone, Fofo County to focus wholeheartedly on my Ripley family, my village of Leone functions, and Siona Le Mauga Pa’ia Congregational Christian Church of Leone until I am called home to serve our Heavenly Father.”

Ms. Ripley received that call in August 2026, bringing full circle a career during which she played a vital supporting role in the evolution of ASCC. 

The administration, faculty and staff of the College offer their most sincere condolences to the Ripley family, and in the words of Interim President Sonny J. Leomiti, “Those of us who knew Cherie, and that is practically all of us, will always remember her with great fondness.”  

[Editor’s Note: Samoa News offers its sincere condolences to Cherie’s family at her passing. She was a friend from days we all began by respecting the journey we each chose to take, the road traveled. While, we did not always stay in contact, whenever met, we greeted each other with a smile full of grace, acknowledging respect for our choices. Manuia lou malaga Cherie — may God’s blessings be yours.]

Local News

Cherie

item.title: 2 Mariners Killed in Strait of Hormuz as Transits See Small Increase
item.description: Two mariners were killed in the past week and a half in the Strait of Hormuz by Iranian attacks. On Monday, an Iranian attack on MV Minoan Dignity in the strait left one seafarer dead. It is the second attack on a ship managed by Greek company Modion Maritime Management. On Aug. 3, MV Minoan Pioneer was struck, with the International Maritime Organization reporting one missing seafarer. It is not clear if the seafarer has been recovered. Two days before the attack on Minoan Dignity, Iran also hit MV Riyan Star in the Strait of Hormuz, killing one crew member.

item.title: Amata highlights Congressional reforms to Medicaid, appreciates CMS Visit
item.description:
Source: Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata’s D.C. staff

Washington, D.C. — Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata’s District Office staff, led by her District Director, Dr. Uta Laloulu Tagoilelagi, met earlier this month with officials from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), to discuss Medicaid services, travel, needs and priorities.

“In recent years, in Congress, we have increased our highest possible availability of Medicaid federal dollars for American Samoa by about ten times the amount it was 12 years ago, and boosted our FMAP from 55 to 83 percent, the highest rate in the nation,” Congresswoman Amata said. “While Congress has improved the big picture, I’m always concerned that the results reach the people who need it most. I appreciate the ongoing work of CMS and ASG to strengthen services and care for our people, but health care challenges here are a constant priority due to our geography and population size,” she continued.

“Thank you to CMS for sending officials to our islands, their willingness to discuss services, and I ask them to continue to look for any and all support they can facilitate for our people. They had a productive discussion in my office, as well as their meeting with ASG officials and Governor Pulaali’i.”

Congressional Medicaid Improvements for American Samoa

    •    Historic reform: Congress passed major bipartisan Medicaid reforms and improvements for American Samoa in 2019, with the support of Congresswoman Amata and other territory representatives.
    •    Ten-fold Increase: This sweeping change went into effect in 2020 and greatly expanded American Samoa’s total available federal funds under the ceiling from $12 million in fiscal year 2019 to over $80 million the very next year, plus yearly increases since indexed to medical inflation rates, currently estimated at $88-90 million – approximately an increase by ten times the amount since fy2015.
    •    83% Match: Under that bipartisan legislation, Congress raised American Samoa’s standard Medicaid federal match (FMAP) to 83 percent under federal statute, up from just 55 percent where it had been for many years.
    •    Long-term Change: Then in 2022, Congress followed up with another major improvement (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023), again with the bipartisan support of Amata and all the territory’s representatives, making American Samoa’s standard 83 percent FMAP rate permanent, no longer at risk of reverting back to 55 percent. This breakthrough means it no longer must be passed over again every few years.
    •    Nation’s Best Rate: American Samoa’s standard federal match (FMAP) is now secure and the highest in the nation – at a better rate than any of the 50 states. The only time the rate can be higher is under a major disaster scenario such as after Storm Gita or during Covid’s peak.
    •    Next effort: Finally, in ongoing work, Amata is an original cosponsor of the bipartisan Medicaid Improvement for Insular Areas Act, H.R. 3154, working together as territories toward removing the Medicaid ceiling entirely, a forward-thinking goal so that American Samoa’s ceiling could never become a future problem. American Samoa’s Medicaid program began in 1983 under a federal funding cap that does not apply to states in the same way, so it is also a matter of principle, to bring about parity with the states on this remaining reform.

Local News
Tags: 
Congresswoman Uifa’atali Amata

item.title: Obituaries for August 21
item.description:
Delbert Chang, 89, of Papaikou died July 24 at Hilo Benioff Medical Center. Born in Waipi‘o Valley, he was a retired butcher for Safeway, a salesman for the former Miko Meats. A 2006 inductee into the big Island Sports Hall of Fame, he was a 156-pound Big Island and territorial champion boxer in the 1950s, and was a longtime volunteer coach for the Wanderers Athletic Club, Papaikou Hongwanji Club, Papaikou Cougars Pop Warner Football and the Big Island Amateur Boxing Association. Visitation 4-6 p.m. Friday (Aug. 28) at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Funeral service at 6 p.m. Graveside committal service 10 a.m. Saturday, Aug. 29, at Homelani Memorial Park, Ilima Section. Casual attire. Survived by daughters, Sheila (Keith) Ogawa and Sharon (Don) Hirota of Hilo, Sandi (Darren) Rosario of Papaikou; brothers, Gilbert (Okyo) Chang and Jerry Chang of Hilo; sister, Shirlene (Leroy) Rayoan of Hilo; sisters-in-law, Promise Grace and Ruth Takayama of Hilo; nine grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren; nieces, nephews and cousins. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for August 21 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Atu‘u land trusteeship meeting moved to September
item.description:
Only five Manu’a matai attended most recent one
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The meeting intended to bring Manu‘a chiefs and residents together to address the Atu‘u land trusteeship has been moved to the second Saturday of September after just five matai arrived at the Office of Samoan Affairs last Friday, prompting officials to postpone the discussion.

Of the five matai who attended, three were Manu‘a’s senators — Ma‘o Fa‘auma Gogo, Tuialu‘ulu‘u Vaimili Tuialu‘ulu‘u, and Misaalefua Hudson — who recommended that the meeting be rescheduled. 

Manu‘a District Governor Poumele Apisa Galea‘i, who chaired the session, agreed to the postponement but informed them he would be traveling to New Zealand on Monday for a medical checkup and would not return until early September.

In an exclusive interview, Poumele said the meeting must include the To‘oto‘o — Manu‘a’s orators who make decisions on behalf of their extended families. 

“The To‘oto‘o and senior matai should be present so it will be a meeting of substance and not one where we just talk, and then nothing happens,” he said. “High Talking Chiefs Malemo and Vaitautolu should have been here today to discuss this issue and bring it to some kind of conclusion.”

He stressed that trustee authorization is the central issue that must be addressed and finalized when the meeting reconvenes for the issue to even move forward.

The initial meeting earlier this month, attended by about 40 Manu'a chiefs and residents, ended with an agreement to reconvene last Friday, August 14, 2026, bringing Manu‘a leadership together in hopes of reaching a consensus on how the Atu‘u trust should be administered going forward — and how lease revenues should be safeguarded for the rightful beneficiaries.

However, only five matai attended.

The Manu‘a District Governor commended the Zoning Board for bringing the issue to the forefront. He said individuals have been signing as the Lessor and collecting lease payments for land that PC Mauga Moimoi conveyed for all the people of Manu‘a under the 1911 trust.

“It’s supposed to be a residential area, but over the years it has been leased out to businesses,” Poumele said. “There shouldn’t be any businesses established there unless authorized by Tufele, who was the Trustee and also the Manu‘a District Governor at the time.”

He noted that the Tufele title has been vacant since Tufele Li‘amatua passed away, and most of the matai and residents who attended the initial meeting agreed that the District Governor should assume the trustee role in the interim. Poumele added that he is also a descendant of the Tufele family through his mother.

Poumele emphasized that serving as Trustee on behalf of an entire community carries responsibilities and obligations to act in the best interest of the people. In this case, he said, lease revenues from the Atu‘u trust land should benefit all Manu‘a residents as stated in the 1911 indenture — not a select few.

“There is so much we can do for the people of Manu‘a using this trust money,” he said, “like establishing scholarships for Manu‘a’s sons and daughters, creating a credit union to help families develop their homes and livelihoods, and funding healthcare services for our elderly.”

Poumele said he has received numerous requests from elderly residents in Manu‘a asking for a dentist to be sent to the island, noting their complaints about having to travel all the way to Tutuila and then wait for hours at LBJ Hospital before receiving any service.

It was agreed that the next meeting should be held on a Saturday, when more people are free to attend, rather than on a weekday.

As a result, it has been scheduled for the second Saturday of September — on the 12th — at the Office of Samoan Affairs.

BACKGROUND

As reported in June by Samoa News, the long‑standing question of who is legally entitled to receive lease payments for land in Atu‘u currently occupied by foreign‑owned businesses resurfaced during a meeting of the American Samoa Zoning Board that month.

The Board reviewed several applications for commercial land lease variances bearing signatures of individuals other than the designated Trust Administrator. Board members questioned whether such private leasing aligns with the 1911 indenture that placed the land “in trust, for the use and benefit of the People of Manu‘a.” 

They argued that the 1911 indenture — a formal, legally binding agreement executed by Paramount Chief Mauga Moimoi, his wife Fa‘apio, and then Manu‘a District Governor Tufele of Si‘ufaga — clearly designates Tufele “as Trustee for the People of Manu‘a.” The indenture conveys the land known as Atu‘u to the trustee and “his successors and assigns forever…IN TRUST, for the USE and BENEFIT of the People of Manu‘a,” establishing that the trustee’s authority overrides any individual’s claim to lease the land.

This prompted Zoning Board member Taesali Sam Matagi — who also chairs the American Samoa Land Commission — to call the initial meeting with the assistance of Secretary of Samoan Affairs Fai‘ivae A. Godinet.

“It was an eye‑opening experience for many Manu‘a residents who did not know the specific terms of the 1911 indenture or the communal rights it established,” Taesali told Samoa News. 

He added that the lack of awareness may not have been accidental. “I suspect the people who were benefiting from lease payments knew,” he said, “but didn’t want to disclose those details. Others may have known but didn’t want to rock the boat because of family ties, or they were receiving some sort of compensation on the side.”

Local News
Tags: 
Atu‘u land

item.description: USS George Washington (CVN-73) arrived in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility yesterday, the combatant command announced on social media. The aircraft carrier, which was accompanied by cruiser USS Robert Smalls (CG-62) and destroyer USS Shoup (DDG-86), transited the Arabian Sea on Thursday, according to the CENTCOM post on social media site X. It is not clear how close GW is to the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group. The George Washington Carrier Strike Group is expected to relieve the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group, but a Navy official could not say when USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) and its escorts

item.title: DOJ argues Comey novel shows he knew ‘86 47’ post was a threat against Trump
item.description:
WASHINGTON — The Justice Department has cited a legal thriller written by James Comey as evidence the former FBI director knew his social media post that featured the numbers “86 47” would be interpreted as a threat against President Donald Trump. U.S. prosecutors, in court filings published late on Tuesday, said Comey’s novel, in which a right-wing podcaster uses coded language to encourage his followers to target political opponents, has parallels with Comey’s 15-month-old post that depicted seashells arranged on a beach to form the numbers “86 47.”

The post DOJ argues Comey novel shows he knew ‘86 47’ post was a threat against Trump appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Obituaries for August 19
item.description:
Glicerio “Lising” Menor Casil, 93, of Pepeekeo died July 30 at Life Care Center of Hilo. Born in Paoay, Ilocos Norte, Philippines, he was a retired seed cutter for the former Mauna Kea Agribusiness, retired foster parent and member of Immaculate Heart of Mary Catholic Church, Pepeekeo Filipino Community Association, Kamana Senior Ballroom Association and Pepeekeo Senior and Pension Club. Visitation 4-6 p.m. Wednesday, Aug. 26, at Dodo Mortuary Chapel. Wake service at 6 p.m. Visitation again 9-9:45 a.m. Thursday, Aug. 27, at Immaculate Heart of Mary Catholic Church in Papaikou. Funeral Mass at 10 a.m. Burial to follow at Alae Cemetery. Casual attire. Survived by wife, Felisa “Fely” Casil of Pepeekeo; daughters, Margarette “Gigi” (David) Parent of Massachusetts and Marissa Ehrenlechner of Pepeekeo; son, Dennis (Heather) Casil of Florida; hanai children, Randall (Kasie) Abadilla of Keaau and Sheena (Cliff Labtis) Buizon of Nevada; sister, Estella Nefalar of Paoay, Philippines; sisters-in-law, Julita Casil, Praxedes Casil and Ofelia Casil; eight grandchildren and eight hanai grandchildren; nieces, nephews and cousins. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary.

The post Obituaries for August 19 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Biden-era ‘ghost guns’ restrictions are unconstitutional, US judge rules
item.description:
A federal judge in Texas has declared that a regulation adopted by Democratic former President Joe Biden’s administration targeting largely untraceable “ghost guns” is unconstitutional — a ruling issued after the U.S. Supreme Court last year upheld the measure. U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor in Fort Worth ruled on Monday that the 2022 rule violates the right to keep and bear arms under the U.S. Constitution’s Second Amendment and was too vague to satisfy the Fifth Amendment’s due process guarantees.

The post Biden-era ‘ghost guns’ restrictions are unconstitutional, US judge rules appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: E-2D Advanced Hawkeye Block II Passes Critical Design Review as Navy Plans to Expand Fleet

item.title: NOAA and partners to explore, map deep waters of American Samoa
item.description:
(Source: NOAA Research Public Affairs)

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — NOAA Ocean Exploration and its partners will conduct two expeditions in waters around American Samoa this summer and fall to map and characterize the deep seafloor in the nation’s highest-priority region for offshore critical mineral exploration.

The expeditions will generate publicly available data and information to increase understanding of mineral potential, guide future exploration, and support federal and local decision-making.

These expeditions will take place aboard NOAA Ship Oceans Explorer. The first will take place August through September 2026 using a remotely operated vehicle (ROV). The second expedition will run from late September through October 2026. Throughout both expeditions, the team will deploy advanced mapping technology and observational sensors. 

“NOAA is dedicating our resources to providing scientific research and data that supports commerce,” said NOAA Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary Erik Noble. “We are investing in the thrill of exploration, tying scientific discoveries to data that industry, government and our partners can use to build prosperity, both at home and around the globe.”

Real-time ROV operations will be streamed online daily.providing the public and shore-based scientists a unique window into the deep-sea environment. This data-driven approach is designed to provide authoritative science for decision-makers at federal and local levels. All data gathered will be made publicly available to support critical mineral assessments, future exploration decisions, and broader marine-resource planning.

“The deep waters around American Samoa hold unknown secrets about our ocean, including unmapped habitats and potential mineral resources critical to our national prosperity and security,” said Captain William Mowitt, acting director of NOAA Ocean Exploration. “By exploring these areas in an open and transparent way, we are providing the authoritative and foundational science that decision-makers and local communities need to responsibly manage the marine environment and its resources.” 

ABOUT THE OKEANOS EXPLORER MISSION IN AMERICAN SAMOA

American Samoa has been identified as the highest-priority region in the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone for mapping and exploration due to its potential for polymetallic nodules and high industry interest. 

This work follows a successful 2026 NOAA-funded project to map and characterize over 30,000 square nautical miles in the region as well as two NOAA-funded expeditions on Ocean Exploration Trust’s Exploration Vessel Nautilus, which included exploration in the eastern American Samoa Exclusive Economic Zone.

Local News
Tags: 
NOAA Ocean Exploration

item.title: Report to Congress on Venezuela and U.S. Policy
item.description: The following is the Aug. 18, 2026, Congressional Research Service report, Venezuela’s Post-Maduro Political Transition and U.S. Policy. From the report Some Members of Congress have closely followed the political and economic situation in Venezuela following the January 3, 2026, U.S. capture and arrest of President Nicolás Maduro (2013-2026) and his wife, Cilia Flores, on narco-terrorism and other charges. Following Maduro’s removal, Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro’s vice president and oil minister of the United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV), took power as acting president. Apparent 2024 election winner Edmundo González Urrutia and opposition leader María Corina Machado have remained in exile.

item.title: Hayden Panettiere, ‘Heroes’ and ‘Nashville’ actress, dies at 36
item.description:
American actress Hayden Panettiere, known for playing a cheerleader with superpowers and a country music star on the television shows “Heroes” and “Nashville” respectively, has died, aged 36, her family said in a statement issued by her publicist on Sunday. The two-time Golden Globe nominee was found unresponsive at an apartment complex in Greenville, South Carolina, and pronounced dead at the scene, the city’s police department said in a statement. Her death was being investigated, but there were no signs of foul play, the police said. An excerpt of a 911 call showed medics confirming to a dispatcher they were responding to an “overdose” at the address and trying to resuscitate an unresponsive woman.

The post Hayden Panettiere, ‘Heroes’ and ‘Nashville’ actress, dies at 36 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Easy dinners for a not-easy time of year
item.description:
I know a lot of people bemoan the fact that holiday commercials, gifty store displays and “however many shopping days until Christmas!” warnings start in October, but I am not one of them. I’ve been known to watch “White Christmas” in July. I shop for my kids’ stocking stuffers year round. And during those dark, lonely days of COVID, I started putting up our Christmas tree on Election Day, and I haven’t gone back.

item.title: Historic Flag Football upset
item.description:
Source: IFAF

DÜSSELDORF, Germany — American Samoa produced one of the biggest victories in its sporting history Friday morning, defeating the defending world champion United States 38–32 at the 2026 IFAF Flag Football World Championships in Düsseldorf.

The result was remarkable not only because of the difference in the two nations’ rankings, but because of the history American Samoa ended.

The United States entered the tournament ranked No. 1 in the world, having won the last five consecutive IFAF Men’s Flag Football World Championships. American Samoa, ranked No. 33, is competing at the world championships for the first time.

Yet when the two teams met in Group A on Friday, it was the small Pacific island territory that emerged with the victory.

USA Football officially lists the final score as American Samoa 38, USA 32. The victory improved American Samoa to 2–0 in Group A, while dropping the United States to 1–1.

A 14-YEAR WAIT

The significance of the victory stretches well beyond the 2026 tournament.

Prior to Friday, the last confirmed defeat for the U.S. men's team at an IFAF World Championship came in the 2012 championship game in Gothenburg, Sweden, when Austria defeated the Americans 47–40.

That game was decided dramatically, with Austria scoring the winning touchdown with only 21 seconds remaining.

USA subsequently captured the world championship in 2014, 2016, 2018, 2021 and 2024, establishing itself as the dominant men's program in international flag football. IFAF described the Americans before this year's tournament as the sport's "gold standard."

American Samoa has now brought that remarkable World Championship run to an end.

And the contrast between the two programs could hardly be greater.

FROM WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP TO DEBUTANT TO GIANT KILLER

American Samoa arrived in Düsseldorf as the lowest-ranked men's team in the tournament and one of the smallest nations competing on the world stage.

The territory has a population of approximately 47,000, and its national flag football program is still in its infancy. IFAF noted before the tournament that American Samoa's delegation had to travel more than 10,000 miles, involving multiple flights and time-zone changes, just to reach Düsseldorf.

American Samoa only entered IFAF international flag football competition in 2025.

But the team immediately showed it belonged.

At the 2025 IFAF Asia-Oceania championships in Ningbo, China, American Samoa defeated New Zealand twice and eventually beat China 41–34 in the bronze-medal game, securing qualification for its first World Championship.

The national federation then guided the team through preparations for Düsseldorf, with American Samoa combining athletes with tackle-football backgrounds with players developing specifically in the five-on-five flag game.

The program also received assistance through the IOC Olympic Solidarity program, which supported athlete development as well as education for coaches and officials in American Samoa.

That development produced an extraordinary result Friday.

AMERICAN SAMOA STARTED SENDING A MESSAGE ON DAY ONE

The victory over the United States was not American Samoa's first surprise of the tournament.

In its opening World Championship game Thursday, American Samoa defeated Oceania champion and world No. 8 Australia 21–7.

That alone was an impressive international debut.

Less than 24 hours later came the breakthrough against the world's No. 1 team.

The matchup was also historic because American Samoa and the United States had never previously faced each other in IFAF competition. IFAF highlighted the matchup before the tournament as one of Group A's intriguing first-time encounters.

USA entered Friday's game after defeating Israel 50–38 in its opener.

American Samoa answered by putting 38 points on the defending champions and holding USA to 32, enough for a six-point victory and a 2–0 start to its first World Championship.

DAVID  VERSUS GOLIATH

Few matchups at these championships could have presented a greater contrast.

USA entered Düsseldorf as the defending world champion, world No. 1, winner of five consecutive world titles, two-time defending Americas champion and winner of the men's competition at the 2022 World Games.

American Samoa entered ranked 33rd and had never played in a World Championship.

Before the tournament, USA head coach Jorge Cascudo made clear that his team intended to continue its championship dominance.

"We have to win the tournament in order to get the bid," Cascudo said while discussing the team's mentality despite USA already having an automatic Olympic berth as the host of Los Angeles 2028. "We want to make sure that we win and continue winning championships and stay on top of flag football."

American Samoa had other plans.

A MILESTONE ON THE ROAD TO LA28

The timing of the victory makes it even more meaningful.

Flag football will make its Olympic debut at the Los Angeles 2028 Games, and the Düsseldorf World Championships are part of the qualification pathway toward that historic tournament.

USA already has its Olympic place as the host nation. For the other countries, Düsseldorf offers the first opportunity to secure Olympic quota places, with the top two eligible men's and women's teams earning berths.

For American Samoa, reaching an Olympic Games in flag football has been identified as a long-term goal of the developing program.

Friday's victory demonstrated that goal may no longer be as distant as many believed.

A country with one of the smallest populations in international sport has now defeated the most successful men's flag football nation of the modern era.

From No. 33 in the world to defeating No. 1.

From playing in its first World Championship to beating the five-time defending champions.

And from a developing flag football program in the middle of the Pacific to producing a result that will resonate throughout the international game.

American Samoa 38. United States 32.

For American Samoa flag football, August 14, 2026, will be remembered as the day the world was put on notice.

That game was decided dramatically, with Austria scoring the winning touchdown with only 21 seconds remaining.
USA subsequently captured the world championship in 2014, 2016, 2018, 2021 and 2024, establishing itself as the dominant men's program in international flag football. IFAF described the Americans before this year's tournament as the sport's "gold standard."
American Samoa has now brought that remarkable World Championship run to an end.
And the contrast between the two programs could hardly be greater.
**FROM WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP TO DEBUTANT TO GIANT KILLER**
American Samoa arrived in Düsseldorf as the lowest-ranked men's team in the tournament and one of the smallest nations competing on the world stage.
The territory has a population of approximately 47,000, and its national flag football program is still in its infancy. IFAF noted before the tournament that American Samoa's delegation had to travel more than 10,000 miles, involving multiple flights and time-zone changes, just to reach Düsseldorf.
American Samoa only entered IFAF international flag football competition in 2025.
But the team immediately showed it belonged.
At the 2025 IFAF Asia-Oceania championships in Ningbo, China, American Samoa defeated New Zealand twice and eventually beat China 41–34 in the bronze-medal game, securing qualification for its first World Championship.
The national federation then guided the team through preparations for Düsseldorf, with American Samoa combining athletes with tackle-football backgrounds with players developing specifically in the five-on-five flag game.
The program also received assistance through the IOC Olympic Solidarity program, which supported athlete development as well as education for coaches and officials in American Samoa.
That development produced an extraordinary result Friday.
**AMERICAN SAMOA STARTED SENDING A MESSAGE ON DAY ONE**
The victory over the United States was not American Samoa's first surprise of the tournament.
In its opening World Championship game Thursday, American Samoa defeated Oceania champion and world No. 8 Australia 21–7.
That alone was an impressive international debut.
Less than 24 hours later came the breakthrough against the world's No. 1 team.
The matchup was also historic because American Samoa and the United States had never previously faced each other in IFAF competition. IFAF highlighted the matchup before the tournament as one of Group A's intriguing first-time encounters.
USA entered Friday's game after defeating Israel 50–38 in its opener.
American Samoa answered by putting 38 points on the defending champions and holding USA to 32, enough for a six-point victory and a 2–0 start to its first World Championship.
**DAVID VERSUS GOLIATH**
Few matchups at these championships could have presented a greater contrast.
USA entered Düsseldorf as the defending world champion, world No. 1, winner of five consecutive world titles, two-time defending Americas champion and winner of the men's competition at the 2022 World Games.
American Samoa entered ranked 33rd and had never played in a World Championship.
Before the tournament, USA head coach Jorge Cascudo made clear that his team intended to continue its championship dominance.
"We have to win the tournament in order to get the bid," Cascudo said while discussing the team's mentality despite USA already having an automatic Olympic berth as the host of Los Angeles 2028. "We want to make sure that we win and continue winning championships and stay on top of flag football."
American Samoa had other plans.
**A MILESTONE ON THE ROAD TO LA28**
The timing of the victory makes it even more meaningful.
Flag football will make its Olympic debut at the Los Angeles 2028 Games, and the Düsseldorf World Championships are part of the qualification pathway toward that historic tournament.
USA already has its Olympic place as the host nation. For the other countries, Düsseldorf offers the first opportunity to secure Olympic quota places, with the top two eligible men's and women's teams earning berths.
For American Samoa, reaching an Olympic Games in flag football has been identified as a long-term goal of the developing program.
Friday's victory demonstrated that goal may no longer be as distant as many believed.
A country with one of the smallest populations in international sport has now defeated the most successful men's flag football nation of the modern era.
From No. 33 in the world to defeating No. 1.
From playing in its first World Championship to beating the five-time defending champions.
And from a developing flag football program in the middle of the Pacific to producing a result that will resonate throughout the international game.
![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
American Samoa 38. United States 32.
For American Samoa flag football, August 14, 2026, will be remembered as the day the world was put on notice.

item.title: AmeriCorps VISTA Award
item.description:
Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Empowering Pacific Island Communities, Inc. (EPIC) is pleased to announce that its AmeriCorps VISTA application for federal assistance has been approved, authorizing three AmeriCorps VISTA members to strengthen organizational and community capacity and expand economic opportunity for low-income individuals and families throughout American Samoa.

The approved project, Empowering Pacific Island Communities, will operate from August 23, 2026 through August 7, 2027 under Project Grant #26VSIAS001.The initiative supports EPIC’s Comprehensive Economic Self- Sufficiency Model by strengthening workforce development, education, caregiver workforce development, community partnerships, outreach, data systems, and long-term organizational sustainability.

EPIC is also pleased to announce the selection of Gina Coffin as its Community Outreach & Public Communication VISTA. Gina brings a background in Health Communications and holds a Bachelor’s degree in Health from New Mexico Highlands University. She will strengthen EPIC’s outreach and communication systems, develop culturally responsive awareness materials and campaigns, enhance social media and stakeholder communications, and expand awareness of workforce, education, caregiver training, and economic self- sufficiency opportunities throughout American Samoa.

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
AmeriCorps

item.title: Butler once again rejected by House for ASEDA board
item.description:
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — The House of Representatives has once more declined to confirm Brett Butler to the Board of Directors of the American Samoa Economic Development Authority (ASEDA), marking the second unsuccessful vote on his appointment in just over a year.

In July of last year, Butler’s nomination fell short when only ten representatives voted in support while seven opposed. House rules require eleven votes for confirmation, leaving Butler one vote shy.

A motion for reconsideration, introduced by Rep. Luaitaua Gene Pan, was approved the same day. The reconsideration vote was held Tuesday, but the outcome remained unchanged — this time, with ten votes against confirmation and eight votes in support.

Butler’s nomination has drawn attention largely because of his extensive background in both the private sector and government finance.

He is a veteran executive with more than 30 years of experience in operations and financial management. Butler was the first local General Manager of StarKist Samoa, serving nine years in the Territory’s largest private‑sector employer. He later joined Bumble Bee Foods, rising through several senior leadership roles, including Vice President of Loining Operations, Vice President & General Manager of the Santa Fe Springs branch, and Vice President of Finance Operations.

After returning to American Samoa, Butler served as Executive Advisor for Finance in the Governor’s Office before being appointed Acting Treasurer in September 2025. His tenure included efforts to modernize ASG’s outdated financial systems, strengthen internal controls, and improve fiscal transparency.

During his confirmation hearing for his appointment as Government Treasurer, legislators described him as a model of local leadership returning home to serve the Territory. Senate Budget Chairman Utu Sila Poasa highlighted Butler’s career trajectory as an example of the kind of expertise American Samoa needs in its financial institutions.

He was unanimously approved by the Senate but fell short of confirmation in the House, a pattern that has been repeated in his nomination to ASEDA Board of Directors.

Supporters had described him as a seasoned executive bringing global industry experience back to the Territory. His nomination to ASEDA was seen as aligning with the authority’s mission of overseeing major financing mechanisms for development projects.

The Senate had previously endorsed Butler’s appointment in March of last year with a unanimous 17 – 0 vote, signaling strong support in the upper chamber. However, ASEDA board appointments require concurrence from both chambers, and the House’s repeated rejection effectively blocks Butler from taking the seat.

With the House denying confirmation for a second time, the administration may submit a new nominee for the ASEDA board seat, attempt another reconsideration if procedurally allowed, or withdraw the nomination entirely.

ASEDA plays a central role in financing major infrastructure and development initiatives, making board appointments closely watched within government and business circles.

 

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
Brett Butler
item.source:markdown:
[![Brett Butler](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/slideshow/public/field/image/butler-senate-200x200.jpeg?itok=zKrkp-Sz)](https://www.samoanews.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_normal_image/public/field/image/butler-senate-200x200.jpeg?itok=prraWdRC)

item.title: USS George Washington Heading West, Lincoln Deployment Nears 9 Months
item.description: The forward-deployed George Washington Carrier Strike Group was in the Strait of Malacca on Thursday, USNI News has learned. Flagship USS George Washington (CVN-73), as well as cruiser USS Robert Smalls (CG-62) and destroyer USS Shoup (DDG-86), were in the Strait of Malacca after making a westbound transit through the Singapore Strait, a Navy official confirmed to USNI News. The Japan-based group is conducting their first patrol of 2026, having departed Yokosuka in May. The George Washington Carrier Strike Group’s transit of the Strait of Malacca comes as the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group’s deployment to continue its extended Middle

item.title: Raised crosswalks draw widespread complaints
item.description:
DPW says they are part of federally funded Islandwide Safety Project
By 
Asi Andrew Fa'asau
andrew@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Senators were informed last Friday that the so‑called “speed bumps,” that are drawing widespread complaints from motorists and lawmakers, are not speed bumps at all, but raised crosswalks — a federally funded safety feature installed as part of the Islandwide Safety Project.

The clarification came during a Senate Public Works Committee hearing, where Deputy Director of Public Works Falava‘i Ta‘ase explained that the raised crosswalks recently constructed in front of Manumalo Academy, SPICC, and Matafao Elementary School were approved and funded by the U.S. Federal Highway Administration (FHWA).

Ta‘ase told senators that FHWA’s push for raised crosswalks is based on national research. A 2016 nationwide study documented a significant rise in pedestrian‑related traffic accidents occurring at traditional painted crosswalks. A follow‑up study in 2023 found a 45% reduction in crosswalk‑related accidents in areas where raised crosswalks were installed.

He said FHWA formally advised Public Works in 2023 to begin evaluating raised crosswalks for American Samoa. The department initially held back, conducting its own assessment of local traffic patterns and crash data. But with traffic accidents increasing last year and again this year, Public Works determined it was time to begin installing raised crosswalks to improve pedestrian safety and reduce vehicle speeds in high‑risk zones.

Ta‘ase explained that the federal criteria for raised crosswalk placement include a speed limit that must be under 30 mph, the traffic volume must be at least 9,000 vehicles, and the roadway must have no more than three lanes.

He said the locations selected so far meet these requirements, particularly school zones where pedestrian traffic is heavy, and vehicle speeds are often higher than posted limits.

Two additional raised crosswalks are scheduled for installation in front of Samoana High School and Marist Saint Francis School in Lepua.

Ta‘ase noted that construction had begun on a raised crosswalk in front of Laufou, but the department halted the project after extended traffic delays created significant congestion. Public Works has decided not to proceed with that location.

Ta‘ase told senators the project was publicly bid, and Paramount Construction was awarded the contract. He estimated the cost of each raised crosswalk at approximately $11,000.

Senate President Tuaolo Manaia Fruean told the Public Works officials that in all his travels across the U.S. mainland, he has never seen road bumps like the ones recently installed. He questioned whether such structures were appropriate for primary roads and asked directly whether the raised crosswalks could be removed.

Deputy Director Ta‘ase confirmed that removal was possible. Tuaolo then advised that they be taken out to put an end to the steady stream of complaints from motorists and community members.

“It’s been nearly 50 years since American Samoa voted for their own governor,” he said. “The question that comes to mind is why now? Why wasn’t this done in all these years? This is very suspicious.”

Senator Magalei Logovii pressed Public Works officials on whether the Department of Public Safety (DPS) had been consulted before the raised crosswalks were installed. He noted that DPS typically provides assessments for any road project, including whether a proposed design might create a traffic hazard or pose risks to pedestrians and motorists.

Magalei repeatedly asked Ta‘ase whether the FHWA had formally approved the raised crosswalks. He requested written documentation from the federal agency confirming its authorization.

Senator Muagututi‘a Tauoa raised additional concerns, warning that the newly installed raised crosswalks could slow or obstruct emergency response vehicles, including EMS ambulances, police units, and the Fire Division. He said any roadway feature that delays emergency response times poses a serious public‑safety risk.

Muagututi‘a also questioned the cost of the installations, noting that at $11,000 per raised crosswalk, the price is “a lot of money” for a project that has already generated significant public frustration. He recommended leaving the three already constructed in place, but urged Public Works not to install any more until the Senate receives clearer justification and documentation from federal authorities.

He also recommended painting the raised crosswalks at Fatu‑ma‑Futi and Matafao to ensure drivers can clearly see them from a distance and recognize when they are approaching a pedestrian zone. 

Muagututi‘a added that proper striping and visibility markings — similar to the treatment already applied to the raised crosswalk in front of Manumalo Academy — are essential for driver awareness and pedestrian safety. He said clear paint markings would help motorists recognize the crosswalks earlier and reduce confusion, especially given the complaints the installations have already generated.

Senator Ma‘o Faauma Gogo, however, sided with Senate President Tuaolo’s recommendation to remove the three raised crosswalks, arguing that traditional street‑sign warnings are sufficient to alert drivers to slow down near schools. He said clear signage has long been effective in school zones and questioned the need for additional roadway structures that have already caused confusion and frustration among motorists.

Ma’o also noted that teachers and students routinely assist with traffic control in front of their schools during morning drop‑off and afternoon pick‑up. He said this long‑standing practice has helped maintain safety without the need for raised crosswalks, and that the community’s involvement demonstrates that simpler, less disruptive measures can work.

Senator Leatualevao Asifoa, who requested the hearing with Public Works, said that based on the photos presented to lawmakers, there appeared to be very little difference between the raised crosswalks and traditional speed bumps. He questioned whether the installations met the design standards described by Public Works.

Senator Togiola T.A. Tulafono echoed those concerns, pointing out that the FHWA design photos showed raised crosswalks with a flat pedestrian surface, whereas the three already constructed in the Territory did not match that profile. He said the discrepancy raised questions about whether the installations were built to federal specifications.

Ta‘ase responded that additional work is planned to bring the crosswalks into compliance. He said the surfaces will be flattened to meet FHWA design requirements and will also be painted to improve visibility and pedestrian safety.

Editor’s Note: Samoa News notes that raised crosswalks are common in other countries, especially in school zones. They are clearly marked, sometimes with special lights (large yellow round bulbs) on each side of the walkway, with the walkway itself characteristically raised and flat, with the traditional stripes defining its width and length. 

The ‘raised’ feature of the crosswalk is to make certain that a vehicle will slow down before proceeding.

Signage include those designating the speed limit as well as warning of approaching crosswalk, and are usually posted on both sides of the road as the raised crosswalk is approached.

There is also sometimes a small planted flower plot area on each side, enhancing the look of the raised crosswalk as a community beautification project.

Local News
Tags: 
Raised crosswalks

item.title: ACLU, others urge judge to block Trump’s latest birthright citizenship orders
item.description:
The ACLU and other groups asked a federal judge to block U.S. President Donald Trump from enforcing new executive orders to limit the number of people eligible for birthright citizenship. In a Tuesday court filing, the groups called Trump’s orders an improper attempt to evade the U.S. Supreme Court’s June 30 rejection of his effort to end birthright citizenship for children whose parents were not American citizens or legal permanent residents, known as green card holders.

item.description:

item.title: Helping ensure Pacific Islander voices are heard
item.description:
By 
Samoa News staff
reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Natalie Tuālemoso Ah Soon, a proud native of Faleasao, Manu‘a, carries the strength of her roots into a life of service and leadership in public health.

 As Director of Community Engagement & Government Relations for RAMS, Inc. in San Francisco, Natalie works at the intersection of community, health and public policy. 

She is also Co-Founder of the Regional Pacific Islander Health Task Force, where she currently serves as Interim Director — helping ensure Pacific Islander voices, experiences and needs are represented where critical health decisions are made. 

She is the daughter of the late Tuālemoso & Katerina Ah Soon.

item.title: Iran ties Hormuz reopening to US concessions on several demands
item.description:
DUBAI/WASHINGTON/CAIRO — Iran said it was nearing a final pact with Oman defining new shipping lanes between them through the Strait of Hormuz but repeated that the U.S. must meet other conditions, including compensation and an end to sanctions and military threats, before the strategic waterway is reopened. A U.S. official told Reuters on Friday that Iran and Oman were close to a deal that could pave the way for restoring safe passage through the strait, a major conduit for oil and gas shipping before Iran blocked Hormuz in response to U.S. and Israeli attacks on Tehran that began in late February. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday an agreement with Oman on the strait was in its “final stages” but reiterated comments made on Saturday that Tehran would not reopen the channel unless the U.S. met certain demands made by Tehran.

The post Iran ties Hormuz reopening to US concessions on several demands appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Obituaries for August 9
item.description:
Marie Lehua Yuriko Ah Yee, 81, of Naalehu died June 25 at home. Born in Pahala, she retired as a machine operator with Mac Farms Of Hawai’i after many years of service. Visitation from 9-10 a.m. on Saturday (Aug. 15). Funeral service at 10 a.m. at Kauaha‘ao Congregational Church, 95-1642 Pinao Street, Naalehu. Reception to follow. Aloha or casual attire requested. Survived by daughter, Stalma (John Self) Ah Yee of Naalehu; brother, Allen Yoshida of Maryland; grandchildren, great-grandchildren and numerous nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary, Inc.

item.title: Senate Republicans narrowly confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general
item.description:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Republicans on Saturday narrowly confirmed Todd Blanche to be President Donald Trump’s attorney general, capping one of the most contentious cabinet fights of Trump’s second term after bipartisan concerns over Blanche’s independence nearly derailed the nomination. Blanche won confirmation in a 50-49 vote, with Republican Senators Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski opposing him. Senator Bill Cassidy was the deciding vote after announcing Friday he thought Blanche was the best option Trump would put forward.

The post Senate Republicans narrowly confirm Todd Blanche as attorney general appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.

item.title: Volcano Watch: Will Kilauea summit lava fountains get taller? Time and chemistry will tell
item.description:
Kilauea’s current summit eruption started on Dec. 23, 2024. Fifty-two episodes of lava fountains have happened on average every 11 days, and we still have many questions about this eruptive behavior. Here, we look at lava fountain heights with magma chemistry to better understand what might be controlling the variability in fountain heights.

item.title: Manumalo Academy student and teacher represent the territory at National History Day Young People’s Continental Congress
item.description:
By 
Samoa News staff
reporters@samoanews.com

Pago Pago, AMERICAN SAMOA — Last month a local student and teacher pair —  Jaceyline Foketi Siliva and Ms. Grace Alesana from Manumalo Academy — represented American Samoa as one of 27 teams from across the US and the world to participate in the third annual Young People's Continental Congress, a joint program during National History Day (NHD).  The event appropriately took place in Philadelphia from July 19 to 25, at Carpenters’ Hall, the home of the nation’s First Continental Congress in 1774.

The Young People’s Continental Congress brought together 27 student-teacher teams from across the country in a study of America’s founding era and democratic ideals and to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. This year’s delegates represent diverse communities across the United States, including American Samoa, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and Department of Defense (DoDEA) schools in the Netherlands and Puerto Rico. 

In preparation for the summer institute, student-teacher teams completed online learning modules throughout spring 2026 on the First Continental Congress and how our founding ideals evolved throughout U.S. history. Once in Philadelphia, teams experienced a week of special programming, including field learning opportunities at Carpenters’ Hall, Independence National Historical Park, the National Constitution Center, the Museum of the American Revolution, and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. During sessions with lead historians and museum professionals, students and teachers participated in discussions about how the ideals of the founding era have continued to be debated and refined over the last 250 years. 

Delegates then co-created and signed a joint declaration of their aspirations for American democracy, just as their historical counterparts issued the Declaration of Colonial Rights and the Declaration of Independence.

“Programs like the Young People’s Continental Congress are fundamental to fostering intergenerational dialogue and much-needed discussions of democratic aspirations from diverse perspectives,” said NHD Executive Director, Dr. Cathy Gorn. “This fantastic group of students and teachers is a reminder of hope for the future, that the next generation is eager to learn about our revolutionary history, reflect on its legacy, and become thoughtful, engaged citizens in the process.”

“It’s so inspiring to watch our young delegates step up to embrace their role as citizens and find their voices,” said Carpenters’ Hall Executive Director, Michael Norris. “This Declaration of Aspirations is also a powerful way for us to remind policymakers and elected officials that young people care deeply about this country and want to be involved in strengthening our democracy.”

Congratulations to all the students and teacher teams who participated in the 2026 Young People’s Continental Congress.

 

Section: 
Local News
Tags: 
NATIONAL HISTORY DAY

item.title: Obituaries for August 7
item.description:
Erlinda Ganal Alejandro, 77, of Kapaau died July 20 at home. Born in Barangay No.6, Sarrat, Ilocos Norte, Philippines, she was a retired pantry worker at Waikoloa Beach Marriott. All-night vigil at 5 p.m. on Friday, Aug. 21, at 53-3980 S. Kahiwa Pl. in Kapaau. Visitation at 8 a.m. on Saturday, Aug. 22, at Sacred Heart Catholic Church in Hawi, with Mass at 10 a.m. Burial to follow at the church cemetery. Casual attire. Flowers welcome. Survived by her daughter, Joycelyn (Joseph) Antonio of Kohala; sons, Jordan (Ronalyn) Alejandro of Kohala and Brian Alejandro of Kohala; stepdaughters, Andrea (Patrick) Brannigan of Kohala and Loretta (Moises) Alejandro of Naples, Fla.; sister, Imelda Hermano of Kohala; grandchildren, great-grandchildren and numerous nieces and nephews. Arrangements by Dodo Mortuary, Inc. – Kona.

The post Obituaries for August 7 appeared first on Hawaii Tribune-Herald.
